newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian deputies revive move to save Lenin's body.
newsitem.headline: Russian deputies revive move to save Lenin's body.

text.p: Russia's communist-led parliament on Wednesday voted to block attempts to bury Bolshevik leader Vladimir Lenin's embalmed body, which still lies in a mausoleum on Red Square 73 years after he died.

Russian parliamentarians also gave strong backing to a bid to bring back the hammer and sickle emblem of the former Soviet Union on Wednesday, but failed to gather enough votes to force through the constitutional changes they sought.

"We appeal to the federal authorities, to the leaders of all parties and movements, to the clergy and religious believers and all honest people to prevent an act of political revenge on V.I. Lenin and to preserve his tomb," the measure said.

The resolution, entitled "Prevent an Act of Vandalism!", failed to win approval on March 21 because not enough deputies were present. But on Wednesday the State Duma lower house passed it by 241 votes to 11.
The pro-government Our Home is Russia party abstained.
The resolution is not legally binding.
The fate of Lenin's body resurfaced as a public issue last month when President Boris Yeltsin floated the idea of a possible referendum on the controversial issue.
Yeltsin said in 1993 he would bury Lenin within weeks. But he then backed off, apparently deciding not to waste political capital on the explosive issue.
Lenin himself wanted to be buried alongside his family in St. Petersburg, according to his wife, Nadezhda Krupskaya, who lobbied the Kremlin after his 1924 death in favour of his burial.

But the vast crowds who came from across Russia to see Lenin's body lying in state inspired Bolshevik leaders to delay the burial and eventually keep it as the most sacred relic of the new state religion of communism.
Today's communists continue to view the preservation of Lenin's body as a matter of great symbolic importance.
Lenin's niece, Olga Ulyanova, added her latest opinion to the debate last week by warning that removing Lenin could "lead to consequences which no one can predict or even imagine".
The mausoleum itself reopened to the public last week after a two-month round of re-embalming which scientists undertake every year or year and half on the 126-year-old body.
Breaking the old secret of the Soviet Union, former embalmers have revealed that during this time Lenin's body is soaked in a tub of chemical solution, then redressed.

During the latest debate in the Duma, a liberal deputy proposed an amendment comparing the possible burial of Lenin with the Communist Party's decision to bury dictator Josef Stalin in 1961, after seven years on public display.
"Of course Boris Yeltsin, a former party boss, would only be following the traditions of the party by burying Lenin," the amendment's author, Sergei Popov, said in debate last month.
Also on Wednesday, the Duma turned its attention to the country's living leaders by asking Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to detail his personal wealth.
The request follows a newspaper report that Chernomyrdin had accumulated vast riches. He denied it.
